newsitem.title: ITALY: League holds "freedom vote" in northern Italy.
newsitem.headline: League holds "freedom vote" in northern Italy.

text.p: Italy's Northern League party held a "referendum" on forming a breakaway northern state on Sunday in a trial of strength with its political opponents.

The League's tough-talking leader Umberto Bossi said in newspaper interviews that the exercise would be a "punch in the teeth" for politicians in the Italian capital and "a step forward on the path to freedom for the North".
Prime Minister Romano Prodi and President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, as well as the Vatican, responded to the challenge with a mixture of mockery and condemnation.
"These things are not serious," Prodi told reporters in the northern city of Bologna. "It (politics) is not one big game."
Scalfaro, a northerner himself, implicitly condemned the League exercise in a speech in Palermo, the capital of the southern island of Sicily.
Without referring to the referendum, he said it was right to seek broad regional autonomy but added that the constitution dictated that Italy should remain "one and indivisible".

The League staged the unofficial plebiscite in 11 of Italy's 20 regions, setting up tents at 13,000 sites as polling stations for voters aged 16 and above to say "Yes" or "No" to its drive for a "federal, independent and sovereign republic of Padania".
Results of the ballot, which has no legal value, are due to be announced on Monday.
Despite assurances of rigorous monitoring, few real controls appeared to have been set up to keep the ballot free of criticism that it would not meet democratic standards.
One Italian journalist who took part in the process was asked for his name, municipality of residence and date of birth but was still able to vote twice at different sites.
Referendum organiser Roberto Maroni estimated that three to four million people among an eligible "electorate" of 22 million had voted by mid-morning. His figures were impossible to verify.
"If it continues like this, we'll probably be able to declare independence tomorrow," he told Italian television.
The League switched to separatism from a federalist agenda last year after it failed to win the balance of power in parliamentary elections despite garnering 10 percent of votes.

A symbolic declaration of independence for "Padania", the name Bossi has given to his nebulous state, flopped last September and the party lost control of Milan, Italy's main northern city, in recent local elections.

Derision of the League's perceived "antics", however, has shifted to real concern since eight separatist paramilitaries occupied the bell tower in the lagoon city of Venice this month to publicise a drive for an independent Venetian republic.
The eight, who went on trial last week, are not directly associated with the League but Bossi's opponents have argued that his secessionist rhetoric has incited hotheads.
The Vatican's semi-official newspaper L'Osservatore Romano called Sunday's exercise not only "absurd...but even more alarming after what happened in Venice".

The League has built support on genuine frustration with past political corruption in Italy and at stifling taxes and an inefficient, highly centralised bureaucracy. It has also sought to exploit prejudice against southerners as lazy and criminal.
The party has so far boycotted an all-party parliamentary commission on constitutional reform, whose brief includes drafting proposals for federal devolution, calling it a sham.
Maroni said the League would submit its own proposals for "real federalism" to the commission this week.
